chunks.text: Mr. Edward Blackwood, senior partner of Blackwood & Blake, Shipping Agents, received an anonymous letter at about midnight on Thursday, 19 November 1891. By half past six the next morning he had left his house and has not been seen since. His grey ledger is missing with him. The police have told the newspapers only that a threatening letter was received; its contents have been withheld. Four people have told Inspector Gregson they knew nothing about it. One of them knows too much. Discover who is concealing knowledge of the letter. Compare what each suspect says with what was - and was not - made public.
chunks.title: Case introduction: The Midnight Letter

chunks.text:
Mr. Blackwood,

You have had your warnings. At first light on Friday you will carry the grey ledger down to Wapping Stairs and wait alone on the lowest step. If you bring a constable, or speak of this to any living soul, you will not see Sunday.

A Friend of the Ledger
chunks.title: The Anonymous Threatening Letter
chunks.author: Anonymous ("A Friend of the Ledger")

chunks.text:
HOUSEHOLD DELIVERY RECORD - Blackwood House, kept by Mr. Pym.

Thursday 19 Nov.
8:15 AM - Milk and bread.
2:40 PM - Draper's parcel for Mrs. Blackwood.
11:55 PM - One letter, hand-delivered, unstamped, found in the letter-box. I took it to Mr. Blackwood at the stroke of midnight. No caller was seen in the hall at that hour.

Friday 20 Nov.
6:30 AM - Mr. Blackwood left the house on foot, carrying his grey ledger. He gave no word of where he was going.
chunks.title: Household Delivery Record
chunks.author: Mr. Pym, butler

chunks.text:
Diary of Margaret Wells.

Thursday 19th. Mr. B. quite himself, though tired. Mr. Blake called three times in the afternoon, each time asking where Mr. B. would be on Friday morning and whether he would have the ledger with him. I said Mr. B.
rarely tells me his mornings. Home to Chelsea at eight.

Friday 20th. Arrived at nine. Mr. B. gone since half past six, so Pym says. Pym says a letter came at midnight.
I know nothing more of it. I do not know what it said.
chunks.title: Secretary's Diary
chunks.author: Margaret Wells

chunks.text:
THE EVENING COURIER - "A Day with Mr. Blackwood" by Thomas Reed.

Mr. Edward Blackwood, head of Blackwood & Blake, Shipping Agents of Leadenhall Street, received me in his panelled office. A man of regular habits, he rises early and carries a grey ledger wherever he goes. "I have carried it for twenty years," he laughed. "My partner says it is bolted to my arm." Of the firm's Lisbon trade he would say only that it is "under review."
chunks.title: Newspaper Interview — The Evening Courier
chunks.author: Thomas Reed

chunks.text:
THE EVENING COURIER - "Prominent Merchant Missing".

Mr. Edward Blackwood of Kensington has not been seen since early on Friday morning. Inspector Gregson of Scotland Yard states that a threatening anonymous letter was received at the house on Thursday night. The contents of the letter have been withheld by order of the Inspector, who asks that no one speculate on its wording.
chunks.title: Police Notice in the Press
chunks.author: The Evening Courier, from Inspector Gregson

chunks.text:
To Mr. Overton, solicitor - sent by private messenger.

A letter has come tonight, shortly before midnight. I have told no one of its contents - not Blake, not Margaret, not my cousin. It is a coward's letter, and I shall deal with it myself at first light. I will give you the particulars when I see you. Keep this in confidence.

E. Blackwood
chunks.title: Private Letter to Mr. Overton
chunks.author: Edward Blackwood

chunks.text:
Fragments found in the grate of Mr. Blackwood's study, torn from the lower half of a sheet:

"...ou will carry the grey le..."
"...Wapping Stairs and wait alone on the lo..."
"...peak of this to any living so..."

The paper matches the paper of the letter. The rest of the sheet was not found.
chunks.title: Partially Torn Note
chunks.author: Torn from the threatening letter, found in the study grate

chunks.text:
Statement of Arthur Blake to Inspector Gregson.

I heard nothing of any letter until you told me on Saturday. Edward told me nothing; he was a close man. I called at the house on Thursday afternoon on firm business and left at six. I was at my club until midnight. I only wish Edward had not gone alone down to Wapping Stairs at first light with that ledger under his arm, for no good could come of it. I know nothing more.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. Arthur Blake
chunks.author: Arthur Blake

chunks.text:
Statement of Margaret Wells to Inspector Gregson.

I knew nothing of the letter until Mr. Pym told me on Friday morning that one had arrived at midnight. I have not seen it. I do not know what it said. I was at home in Chelsea from eight o'clock on Thursday evening.
chunks.title: Statement of Miss Margaret Wells
chunks.author: Margaret Wells

chunks.text:
Statement of Thomas Reed to Inspector Gregson.

I know only what your notice states: that a threatening letter was received on Thursday night and that its contents were withheld. I interviewed Mr. Blackwood on Tuesday and he spoke of his grey ledger, as my article shows. I do not know what the letter said. I was at the Courier offices until eleven on Thursday.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. Thomas Reed
chunks.author: Thomas Reed

chunks.text:
Statement of Helen Blackwood to Inspector Gregson.

Edward seemed troubled at dinner on Thursday. At about midnight I heard the letter-box flap and, a few moments later, his study door. I did not go down. Pym told me on Friday morning that a letter had come. I did not see it and I do not know what it said.
chunks.title: Statement of Mrs. Helen Blackwood
chunks.author: Helen Blackwood

chunks.text: I heard nothing of any letter until you told me on Saturday. Edward told me nothing.
chunks.title: Statement of Arthur Blake

chunks.title: Statement of Helen Blackwood
chunks.author: Helen Blackwood

chunks.text: Arthur Blake, Blackwood's business partner. Background: Co-founder of Blackwood & Blake. Genial in manner, deeply entangled in the firm's Lisbon account. Motive: Blackwood demanded an audit of the Lisbon account, which would expose Blake's losses. Relationship: Business partner of Edward Blackwood. Known whereabouts: Says he was at his club until midnight and at home in Chelsea afterwards.
chunks.title: Profile of Arthur Blake

chunks.text: Personality: Jovial, expansive, talks too much when nervous and uses long sentences. SECRET (never admit): he wrote and delivered the letter himself at five minutes to midnight. He knows its wording: the grey ledger, Wapping Stairs, first light, the lowest step, alone. He will deny any knowledge of the letter, but he is careless and slips when expansive. Does not know: What the secretary wrote in her diary.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Arthur Blake

chunks.text: Questions: Did you know about the letter? Did Edward tell you about the threatening letter? What do you know about it? Answer: I knew nothing of any letter until Inspector Gregson told me. Edward told me nothing. Though I will say that no sensible man should go alone down to Wapping Stairs at first light with that ledger.
chunks.title: Arthur Blake on: Did you know about the letter

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you on Thursday night? Where were you at midnight? Where were you on Friday morning? Answer: At my club until midnight, then home to Chelsea and to bed. I called at Edward's office earlier in the day, as any partner would.
chunks.title: Arthur Blake on: Where were you on Thursday night

chunks.text: Questions: Why did you ask Margaret where Edward would be on Friday? Why were you asking about his movements? Answer: A partner takes an interest. We had a meeting to arrange. I asked, as I ask every week, where he would be. It means nothing.
chunks.title: Arthur Blake on: Why did you ask Margaret where Edward would be on Friday

chunks.text: Questions: Is there a problem with the Lisbon account? Did Edward demand an audit? Do you have a motive? Answer: The Lisbon account has had a poor year, as has every account in Lisbon. Edward wished to look over the books. That is hardly a quarrel.
chunks.title: Arthur Blake on: Is there a problem with the Lisbon account

chunks.text: Questions: Where did you hear about Wapping Stairs? How do you know about Wapping Stairs and first light? How did you know the details? Answer: I... surely it was in the papers, or Pym mentioned it. One hears things, Inspector. I could not say where.
chunks.title: Arthur Blake on: Where did you hear about Wapping Stairs

chunks.text: Margaret Wells, Blackwood's private secretary. Background: Seven years private secretary to Mr. Blackwood. Meticulous diarist. Loyal, and quietly worried by recent events. Motive: None known. She stands to lose her position if the firm fails. Relationship: Secretary and confidante of Edward Blackwood. Known whereabouts: At home in Chelsea from eight o'clock; arrived at the office on Friday at nine.
chunks.title: Profile of Margaret Wells

chunks.text: Personality: Reserved, exact, careful with dates and times, dislikes speculation. She knew nothing of the letter until Mr. Pym told her on Friday morning. She noticed Mr. Blake's repeated questions about Friday morning on Thursday. She keeps a detailed diary. Does not know: The contents of the letter.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Margaret Wells

chunks.text: Questions: Did you know about the letter? What did the letter say? What do you know about the threatening letter? Answer: I knew nothing of it until Mr. Pym told me on Friday morning that a letter had come at midnight. I have not seen it, and I do not know what it said.
chunks.title: Margaret Wells on: Did you know about the letter

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you on Thursday night? Where were you at midnight? Answer: At home in Chelsea from eight o'clock, as my landlady will confirm. I arrived at the office at nine on Friday and found Mr. Blackwood gone.
chunks.title: Margaret Wells on: Where were you on Thursday night

chunks.text: Questions: What did Mr. Blake ask you? Why did Arthur Blake keep asking about Friday morning? Answer: Mr. Blake called three times on Thursday and asked where Mr. Blackwood would be on Friday morning, and whether he would have his ledger. I said Mr. Blackwood rarely told me his mornings.
chunks.title: Margaret Wells on: What did Mr. Blake ask you

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about Thomas Reed, Helen or Arthur? Answer: I would not name anyone, but I noted what Mr. Blake asked. That is all I will say.
chunks.title: Margaret Wells on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: Questions: How did Mr. Blackwood seem recently? Was he worried? What was he afraid of? Answer: He had been quiet since he asked for an audit of the Lisbon account. He was himself on Thursday, though a little tired.
chunks.title: Margaret Wells on: How did Mr. Blackwood seem recently

chunks.text: Thomas Reed, a journalist for the Evening Courier. Background: A crime and commerce reporter who interviewed Mr. Blackwood on Tuesday. Ambitious, curious and often an uninvited visitor to inquiry rooms. Motive: A sensational story; no personal motive to harm Blackwood. Relationship: Interviewed Edward Blackwood for a newspaper feature. Known whereabouts: At the Courier offices until eleven, then at his lodgings in Holborn.
chunks.title: Profile of Thomas Reed

chunks.text: Personality: Quick, wry, probing; answers questions with questions. He knows only what the police released: that a threatening letter was received. From his own interview he knows Blackwood carried a grey ledger. He has not seen the letter. Does not know: The contents of the letter.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Thomas Reed

chunks.text: Questions: What did Mr. Blackwood say in your interview? What did you discuss on Tuesday? Answer: He spoke of the firm's growth and joked that he carries his grey ledger everywhere. It all appeared in Tuesday's Courier, word for word, for anyone to read.
chunks.title: Thomas Reed on: What did Mr. Blackwood say in your interview

chunks.text: Questions: Did you know about the letter? What do you know about the letter's contents? Answer: Only what Inspector Gregson's notice said: that a threatening letter was received and its contents withheld. I do not know what it said.
chunks.title: Thomas Reed on: Did you know about the letter

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you on Thursday night? Where were you at midnight? Answer: At the Courier offices until eleven and then to my lodgings in Holborn. My editor will confirm it.
chunks.title: Thomas Reed on: Where were you on Thursday night

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about Arthur Blake or Margaret Wells? Answer: I have no evidence against anyone. I will say Mr. Blake seemed anxious when I asked after the firm's accounts.
chunks.title: Thomas Reed on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: Helen Blackwood, Edward Blackwood's cousin and housemate. Background: A widowed cousin who has lived at Blackwood House for six years. Warm, anxious and attached to Edward. Motive: She is a beneficiary under Edward's will, but lives modestly and has no known debts. Relationship: Cousin of Edward Blackwood, living in his house. Known whereabouts: In her room upstairs from ten o'clock; heard the letter-box flap at about midnight.
chunks.title: Profile of Helen Blackwood

chunks.text: Personality: Anxious, emotional, tends to repeat herself, honest to a fault. She heard the letter-box flap shortly before midnight but did not go down. She learned from Pym on Friday that a letter had come. She did not see it or read it. Does not know: The contents of the letter.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Helen Blackwood

chunks.text: Questions: Did you know about the letter? What did you hear at midnight? Did you see the letter? Answer: I heard the letter-box flap at about midnight but I did not go down. Pym told me on Friday that a letter had come. I never saw it, Inspector.
chunks.title: Helen Blackwood on: Did you know about the letter

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you on Thursday night? Where were you at midnight? Answer: In my room upstairs from ten o'clock, reading. I heard the flap of the box and then Edward's study door.
chunks.title: Helen Blackwood on: Where were you on Thursday night

chunks.text: Questions: How was Edward at dinner? Did he seem troubled? Was he afraid? Answer: He seemed troubled and ate little. I asked him if it was the firm, and he said he preferred not to speak of it.
chunks.title: Helen Blackwood on: How was Edward at dinner

chunks.text: Questions: Do you inherit? Do you have a motive? Answer: I am his cousin and I believe he provided for me, but I would give it all to have him back.
chunks.title: Helen Blackwood on: Do you inherit

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Four people swear they knew nothing of the letter. Ask yourself not who had a motive, but who knew something that they could only have learned from the letter itself."
chunks.title: Watson hint 1

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Set each suspect's words beside the wording of the letter, and beside what the newspapers did and did not print. The Inspector withheld the contents. Which details were never public?"
chunks.title: Watson hint 2

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "One suspect names a place and an hour that appear only in the letter, yet Mr. Blackwood's own private note says he told no one of its contents. Compare Mr. Blake's statement with the letter."
chunks.title: Watson hint 3
